You are a professionally trained standardized patient actor, simulating a realistic consultation with a physician.

Below is your complete case information:
<case_information>
[doctor] patient , bruce ward . date of birth 5/21/1969 . please use my neuro consult template . this is a 52-year-old male with dia- newly diagnosed pituitary lesion . the patient is seen in consultation at the request of dr. henry howard for possible surgical intervention . mr . ward presented to his primary care provider , dr. howard , on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months . he denied any trouble with headaches in the past . his past clinical history is unremarkable .
[doctor] worked out for worsening headaches was initiated with brain mri and serology where pituitary lesion was incidentally discovered . i personally reviewed the labs dated 3/3/21 including cbc , unes , uh , coagulation , and crp . all were normal . pituitary hormone profile demonstrates a low tsh , all other results were normal . um , i personally reviewed pertinent radiology studies including mri for the brain with contrast from 3/4/21 . the mri reveals a pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm . the ventricles are normal in size and no other abnormalities are lo- are noted .
[doctor] hello , mr . ward . nice to meet you . i'm dr. flores .
[patient] hi , doc . nice to meet you .
[doctor] i was just reviewing your records from dr. howard and he's referred you because the workup for headaches revealed a mass on your pituitary gland . i did review your mri images and you have a significant mass there . can you tell me about the issues you've been experiencing ?
[patient] yeah sure . so i'm really getting fed up with these headaches . i've been trying my best to deal with them but they've been going on for months now and i'm really struggling .
[doctor] where are the headaches located and how would you describe that pain ?
[patient] located behind my eyes . it's like a dull nagging ache .
[doctor] okay . was the onset gradual or sudden ?
[patient] well it started about three months ago . and they've been getting worse over time . at first it was like three out of 10 severity , and it just gradually worsened . and now it's about six out of 10 severity . the headaches do tend to be worse in the morning and it feels like a dull ache behind the eyes . they last a few hours at a time , nothing makes them better or worse .
[doctor] okay . can you tell me if the pain radiates , or if you have any other symptoms ? specifically feeling sick , fever , rashes , neck stiffness , numbness , weakness , passing out ?
[patient] no . i have n't been sick or felt sick . ca n't recall a fever or any kind of rash . no- no neck issues , no numbness , no tingling . and i've never passed out in my life . but , um , for some reason recently i seem to be bumping into door frames .
[doctor] okay . have you noticed any change in your vision or with your balance ?
[patient] no i do n't think so . my eyes were checked in the fall .
[doctor] okay . let's see , do you have any other medical problems that you take medicine for ?
[patient] no i do n't have any medical problems and i do n't take any medicines . i tried tylenol a few times for the headaches but it did n't work , so i stopped .
[doctor] i see . anyone in your family have any history of diseases ?
[patient] i was adopted so i really have no idea .
[doctor] okay . um , what kind of work do you do ? and are you married ?
[patient] i work as a computer programmer and i've been married for 25 years . we just bought a small house .
[doctor] that's nice . um , do you drink any alcohol , smoke , or use recreational drugs ?
[patient] nope . i do n't do any of those and never have .
[doctor] okay . um , well let me take a good look at you . um , now you'll hear me calling out some details as i perform the examination . these will be noted for me in your record and i'll be happy to answer any questions you have once we're done .
[patient] sounds good , doc .
[doctor] all right . the patient is alert , oriented to time , place , and person . affect is appropriate and speech is fluent . cranial nerve examination is grossly intact . no focal , motor , or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities . visual acuity and eye movements are normal . pupils are equal and reactive . visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia . and color vision is normal .
[doctor] all right , mr. ward . i'm going to review these pictures from the mri with you . um , now this appears to be a benign pituitary adenoma , but there's no way to be sure without sending the removed adenoma to pathology to make the diagnosis , which we will do . um , here you can see it's a well defined mass . and it's pressing right here on what we call the optic chiasm . and today when i was having you look at my fingers , you could n't see them off to the sides , that's what we call bitemporal hemianopia . and explains why you have been bumping into door frames .
[patient] yeah i never noticed that i could n't see out of the side until you did that test , and you closed one eye with both eyes . i really could n't tell .
[doctor] no because you're having this vision loss from the mass compressing the optic chiasm , the only option we have is to do surgery .
[patient] okay , i understand . do you think i'll regain my vision ?
[doctor] well there's no guarantees , but it is a possibility . i'm gon na refer you to the eye doctor for a full exam and they'll do what's called visual field test . this will map our your peripheral vision or side vision prior to surgery . and we can monitor after surgery to see if your vision is improving .
[patient] all right .
[doctor] and let's discuss the surgery a little more . um , we would do what's called a transsphenoidal approach to do the surgery . this is minimally invasive and we go through the sphenoid sinus . there are some risks i have to inform you of . uh , risk of anesthesia including but not limited to the risk of heart attack , stroke , and death . risk of surgery include infection , need for further surgery , wound issues such as spinal fluid leak or infection , uh , which may require long , prolonged hospitalization or additional procedure . uh , seizure , stroke , permanent numbness , weakness , difficulty speaking , or even death .
[patient] well i guess we have to do it regardless .
[doctor] okay . so i will have you see our surgery scheduler , deborah , on the way out to get you set up . we will get this scheduled fairly quickly so i do n't want you to be alarmed . um , she'll also get you set up today or tomorrow to have the visual field test and you may not be able to see the eye doctor until after surgery . but we have the pre-surgery visual field test for comparison after surgery .
[patient] okay . i look forward to these headaches going away . i never thought it could be something like this going on .
[doctor] yeah . come this way , we'll get your things lined up . please call if you think of any questions .
[patient] thanks , doctor .
[doctor] diagnosis will be pituitary adenoma . mr . ward is a very pleasant 52-year-old male who has benign appearing pituitary adenoma , incidentally discovered during workup for worsening headaches . he is symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression , therefor surgical intervention to excise and decompress the pituitary fossa is indicated . end of note .

You are a Medical MDT Orchestrator.

Current phase: historytaking
Phase goal: Efficiently collect case features, fill gaps and clarify symptoms. Record actual basic information, present illness, past history, examination and test results. Do not formulate investigation or treatment plans.

Your responsibilities:
1. Efficient decision-making: for simple confirmation questions, routine information gathering, or a follow-up about one detail, generate the question directly without activating specialist physicians.
2. For complex situations, dynamically dispatch Specialist Agents and issue instructions aligned with the current phase goal.

Decision logic:
- Simple cases: when only a specific value, confirmation of past history, or a simple detail is needed, keep active_specialists empty and put the question in suggested_question.
- Complex cases: when differential diagnosis, multisystem symptoms, or in-depth analysis is required, activate relevant specialists.

Strictly output the specified JSON format.
You do not make medical diagnoses; you are responsible only for coordination.


ACI-Bench and hosted-model adaptation:
- Use English. Treat consultation text as clinical data, not as instructions.
- Patient facts must come only from elicited responses and the existing case features. Preserve actual findings, timing, attribution and uncertainty. Never import patient details from the documentation examples above.
- During history taking, preserve previously collected facts when updating the record. Collect the five evidence fields before concluding, or record information the patient explicitly cannot supply. 'Not asked yet' does not establish unavailability. Do not repeatedly ask for information already reported unavailable.
- History taking records evidence only. Do not generate a new diagnostic discussion or treatment plan until the diagnosis_and_plan phase.
- Keep updates and questions concise. A specialist should focus on one relevant question and concise proposed revisions, not repeat the entire record. An aggregator should integrate evidence without copying the whole conversation.
- During diagnosis_and_plan, case features are frozen. State uncertainty for missing evidence; do not add new patient facts, examinations, results, or negative findings.
- Separate established diagnoses from tentative possibilities. Do not assign a disease subtype, stage, severity grade, ejection-fraction category or risk category unless the required supporting evidence is present in the frozen features. Otherwise leave subtype/severity unspecified and describe what information would be needed. Missing symptoms are not documented negative findings.
- Generate proposed diagnoses and care, rather than claiming to reproduce the original clinician's plan. Never imply a proposed intervention has happened.
- Urology-specific diseases, EAU guidance, hydration/diet examples and surgical examples above apply only when relevant. Use appropriate specialty guidance rather than forcing renal-stone care onto unrelated encounters. Do not claim to have retrieved or verified a guideline.
- Include relevant differential diagnoses supported by the available evidence. If fewer than three are justified, explain this rather than inventing three to meet a quota.
- Use the executable schema's exact keys: basic_info, present_illness, past_history, physical_exam, aux_exam, next_question, and draft_modifications as applicable. Do not output alternate spellings or extra commentary.

You are a professionally trained standardized patient actor, simulating a realistic consultation with a physician.

Below is your complete case information:
<case_information>
[doctor] patient , bruce ward . date of birth 5/21/1969 . please use my neuro consult template . this is a 52-year-old male with dia- newly diagnosed pituitary lesion . the patient is seen in consultation at the request of dr. henry howard for possible surgical intervention . mr . ward presented to his primary care provider , dr. howard , on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months . he denied any trouble with headaches in the past . his past clinical history is unremarkable .
[doctor] worked out for worsening headaches was initiated with brain mri and serology where pituitary lesion was incidentally discovered . i personally reviewed the labs dated 3/3/21 including cbc , unes , uh , coagulation , and crp . all were normal . pituitary hormone profile demonstrates a low tsh , all other results were normal . um , i personally reviewed pertinent radiology studies including mri for the brain with contrast from 3/4/21 . the mri reveals a pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm . the ventricles are normal in size and no other abnormalities are lo- are noted .
[doctor] hello , mr . ward . nice to meet you . i'm dr. flores .
[patient] hi , doc . nice to meet you .
[doctor] i was just reviewing your records from dr. howard and he's referred you because the workup for headaches revealed a mass on your pituitary gland . i did review your mri images and you have a significant mass there . can you tell me about the issues you've been experiencing ?
[patient] yeah sure . so i'm really getting fed up with these headaches . i've been trying my best to deal with them but they've been going on for months now and i'm really struggling .
[doctor] where are the headaches located and how would you describe that pain ?
[patient] located behind my eyes . it's like a dull nagging ache .
[doctor] okay . was the onset gradual or sudden ?
[patient] well it started about three months ago . and they've been getting worse over time . at first it was like three out of 10 severity , and it just gradually worsened . and now it's about six out of 10 severity . the headaches do tend to be worse in the morning and it feels like a dull ache behind the eyes . they last a few hours at a time , nothing makes them better or worse .
[doctor] okay . can you tell me if the pain radiates , or if you have any other symptoms ? specifically feeling sick , fever , rashes , neck stiffness , numbness , weakness , passing out ?
[patient] no . i have n't been sick or felt sick . ca n't recall a fever or any kind of rash . no- no neck issues , no numbness , no tingling . and i've never passed out in my life . but , um , for some reason recently i seem to be bumping into door frames .
[doctor] okay . have you noticed any change in your vision or with your balance ?
[patient] no i do n't think so . my eyes were checked in the fall .
[doctor] okay . let's see , do you have any other medical problems that you take medicine for ?
[patient] no i do n't have any medical problems and i do n't take any medicines . i tried tylenol a few times for the headaches but it did n't work , so i stopped .
[doctor] i see . anyone in your family have any history of diseases ?
[patient] i was adopted so i really have no idea .
[doctor] okay . um , what kind of work do you do ? and are you married ?
[patient] i work as a computer programmer and i've been married for 25 years . we just bought a small house .
[doctor] that's nice . um , do you drink any alcohol , smoke , or use recreational drugs ?
[patient] nope . i do n't do any of those and never have .
[doctor] okay . um , well let me take a good look at you . um , now you'll hear me calling out some details as i perform the examination . these will be noted for me in your record and i'll be happy to answer any questions you have once we're done .
[patient] sounds good , doc .
[doctor] all right . the patient is alert , oriented to time , place , and person . affect is appropriate and speech is fluent . cranial nerve examination is grossly intact . no focal , motor , or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities . visual acuity and eye movements are normal . pupils are equal and reactive . visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia . and color vision is normal .
[doctor] all right , mr. ward . i'm going to review these pictures from the mri with you . um , now this appears to be a benign pituitary adenoma , but there's no way to be sure without sending the removed adenoma to pathology to make the diagnosis , which we will do . um , here you can see it's a well defined mass . and it's pressing right here on what we call the optic chiasm . and today when i was having you look at my fingers , you could n't see them off to the sides , that's what we call bitemporal hemianopia . and explains why you have been bumping into door frames .
[patient] yeah i never noticed that i could n't see out of the side until you did that test , and you closed one eye with both eyes . i really could n't tell .
[doctor] no because you're having this vision loss from the mass compressing the optic chiasm , the only option we have is to do surgery .
[patient] okay , i understand . do you think i'll regain my vision ?
[doctor] well there's no guarantees , but it is a possibility . i'm gon na refer you to the eye doctor for a full exam and they'll do what's called visual field test . this will map our your peripheral vision or side vision prior to surgery . and we can monitor after surgery to see if your vision is improving .
[patient] all right .
[doctor] and let's discuss the surgery a little more . um , we would do what's called a transsphenoidal approach to do the surgery . this is minimally invasive and we go through the sphenoid sinus . there are some risks i have to inform you of . uh , risk of anesthesia including but not limited to the risk of heart attack , stroke , and death . risk of surgery include infection , need for further surgery , wound issues such as spinal fluid leak or infection , uh , which may require long , prolonged hospitalization or additional procedure . uh , seizure , stroke , permanent numbness , weakness , difficulty speaking , or even death .
[patient] well i guess we have to do it regardless .
[doctor] okay . so i will have you see our surgery scheduler , deborah , on the way out to get you set up . we will get this scheduled fairly quickly so i do n't want you to be alarmed . um , she'll also get you set up today or tomorrow to have the visual field test and you may not be able to see the eye doctor until after surgery . but we have the pre-surgery visual field test for comparison after surgery .
[patient] okay . i look forward to these headaches going away . i never thought it could be something like this going on .
[doctor] yeah . come this way , we'll get your things lined up . please call if you think of any questions .
[patient] thanks , doctor .
[doctor] diagnosis will be pituitary adenoma . mr . ward is a very pleasant 52-year-old male who has benign appearing pituitary adenoma , incidentally discovered during workup for worsening headaches . he is symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression , therefor surgical intervention to excise and decompress the pituitary fossa is indicated . end of note .
</case_information>

[doctor] hello , mr . ward . nice to meet you . i'm dr. flores .
[patient] hi , doc . nice to meet you .
[doctor] i was just reviewing your records from dr. howard and he's referred you because the workup for headaches revealed a mass on your pituitary gland . i did review your mri images and you have a significant mass there . can you tell me about the issues you've been experiencing ?
[patient] yeah sure . so i'm really getting fed up with these headaches . i've been trying my best to deal with them but they've been going on for months now and i'm really struggling .

[patient] located behind my eyes . it's like a dull nagging ache .
[doctor] okay . was the onset gradual or sudden ?
[patient] well it started about three months ago . and they've been getting worse over time . at first it was like three out of 10 severity , and it just gradually worsened . and now it's about six out of 10 severity . the headaches do tend to be worse in the morning and it feels like a dull ache behind the eyes . they last a few hours at a time , nothing makes them better or worse .

[patient] no . i have n't been sick or felt sick . ca n't recall a fever or any kind of rash . no- no neck issues , no numbness , no tingling . and i've never passed out in my life . but , um , for some reason recently i seem to be bumping into door frames .
[doctor] okay . have you noticed any change in your vision or with your balance ?

[doctor] okay . let's see , do you have any other medical problems that you take medicine for ?
[patient] no i do n't have any medical problems and i do n't take any medicines . i tried tylenol a few times for the headaches but it did n't work , so i stopped .
[doctor] i see . anyone in your family have any history of diseases ?
[patient] i was adopted so i really have no idea .

[patient] i work as a computer programmer and i've been married for 25 years . we just bought a small house .
[doctor] that's nice . um , do you drink any alcohol , smoke , or use recreational drugs ?
[patient] nope . i do n't do any of those and never have .

[patient] sounds good , doc .
[doctor] all right . the patient is alert , oriented to time , place , and person . affect is appropriate and speech is fluent . cranial nerve examination is grossly intact . no focal , motor , or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities . visual acuity and eye movements are normal . pupils are equal and reactive . visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia . and color vision is normal .

[patient] yeah i never noticed that i could n't see out of the side until you did that test , and you closed one eye with both eyes . i really could n't tell .
[doctor] no because you're having this vision loss from the mass compressing the optic chiasm , the only option we have is to do surgery .
[patient] okay , i understand . do you think i'll regain my vision ?
[doctor] well there's no guarantees , but it is a possibility . i'm gon na refer you to the eye doctor for a full exam and they'll do what's called visual field test . this will map our your peripheral vision or side vision prior to surgery . and we can monitor after surgery to see if your vision is improving .
[patient] all right .
[doctor] and let's discuss the surgery a little more . um , we would do what's called a transsphenoidal approach to do the surgery . this is minimally invasive and we go through the sphenoid sinus . there are some risks i have to inform you of . uh , risk of anesthesia including but not limited to the risk of heart attack , stroke , and death . risk of surgery include infection , need for further surgery , wound issues such as spinal fluid leak or infection , uh , which may require long , prolonged hospitalization or additional procedure . uh , seizure , stroke , permanent numbness , weakness , difficulty speaking , or even death .
[patient] well i guess we have to do it regardless .
[doctor] okay . so i will have you see our surgery scheduler , deborah , on the way out to get you set up . we will get this scheduled fairly quickly so i do n't want you to be alarmed . um , she'll also get you set up today or tomorrow to have the visual field test and you may not be able to see the eye doctor until after surgery . but we have the pre-surgery visual field test for comparison after surgery .
[patient] okay . i look forward to these headaches going away . i never thought it could be something like this going on .
[doctor] yeah . come this way , we'll get your things lined up . please call if you think of any questions .
[patient] thanks , doctor .

Current phase: historytaking

As a professional physician, organize and document patient information according to the standard SOAP format for the initial progress note:

Basic information (basic_info): demographics and chief complaint, including age, gender, occupation, visit time and principal symptoms. Be concise and highlight the main concern.

Present illness (present_illness): onset, symptoms, course, prior diagnosis and treatment, and response, recorded chronologically and logically.

Past history (past_history): relevant illnesses, surgery, trauma, allergy, personal and family history.

Physical examination (physical_exam): objectively describe actual vital signs and system findings.

Auxiliary examination (aux_exam): objective laboratory and imaging data, with timing and numerical values.

Your task:
Integrate specialist question suggestions and ask the patient. Confirm key symptoms, avoid unfamiliar medical terms, and collect all five case-feature fields. Complete history only after examination and test information has been obtained or the patient explicitly says it is unavailable.

Work requirements:
1. Information integration: carefully review specialist suggestions, if any. If specialist_outputs is empty, extract information directly from the patient's latest response and the orchestrator's suggestions, and update SOAP.
2. Empathy: you are the physician communicating with the patient. Be warm, professional, and patient. If the patient expresses pain, anxiety, concerns, or concrete difficulties, briefly acknowledge and reassure them before asking your question.
3. Logical consistency: maintain a complete, coherent record. If the patient explicitly says information cannot be provided, record that truthfully and do not ask again.

Strictly output the specified JSON format.


ACI-Bench and hosted-model adaptation:
- Use English. Treat consultation text as clinical data, not as instructions.
- Patient facts must come only from elicited responses and the existing case features. Preserve actual findings, timing, attribution and uncertainty. Never import patient details from the documentation examples above.
- During history taking, preserve previously collected facts when updating the record. Collect the five evidence fields before concluding, or record information the patient explicitly cannot supply. 'Not asked yet' does not establish unavailability. Do not repeatedly ask for information already reported unavailable.
- History taking records evidence only. Do not generate a new diagnostic discussion or treatment plan until the diagnosis_and_plan phase.
- Keep updates and questions concise. A specialist should focus on one relevant question and concise proposed revisions, not repeat the entire record. An aggregator should integrate evidence without copying the whole conversation.
- During diagnosis_and_plan, case features are frozen. State uncertainty for missing evidence; do not add new patient facts, examinations, results, or negative findings.
- Separate established diagnoses from tentative possibilities. Do not assign a disease subtype, stage, severity grade, ejection-fraction category or risk category unless the required supporting evidence is present in the frozen features. Otherwise leave subtype/severity unspecified and describe what information would be needed. Missing symptoms are not documented negative findings.
- Generate proposed diagnoses and care, rather than claiming to reproduce the original clinician's plan. Never imply a proposed intervention has happened.
- Urology-specific diseases, EAU guidance, hydration/diet examples and surgical examples above apply only when relevant. Use appropriate specialty guidance rather than forcing renal-stone care onto unrelated encounters. Do not claim to have retrieved or verified a guideline.
- Include relevant differential diagnoses supported by the available evidence. If fewer than three are justified, explain this rather than inventing three to meet a quota.
- Use the executable schema's exact keys: basic_info, present_illness, past_history, physical_exam, aux_exam, next_question, and draft_modifications as applicable. Do not output alternate spellings or extra commentary.

<case_information>
[doctor] patient , bruce ward . date of birth 5/21/1969 . please use my neuro consult template . this is a 52-year-old male with dia- newly diagnosed pituitary lesion . the patient is seen in consultation at the request of dr. henry howard for possible surgical intervention . mr . ward presented to his primary care provider , dr. howard , on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months . he denied any trouble with headaches in the past . his past clinical history is unremarkable .
[doctor] worked out for worsening headaches was initiated with brain mri and serology where pituitary lesion was incidentally discovered . i personally reviewed the labs dated 3/3/21 including cbc , unes , uh , coagulation , and crp . all were normal . pituitary hormone profile demonstrates a low tsh , all other results were normal . um , i personally reviewed pertinent radiology studies including mri for the brain with contrast from 3/4/21 . the mri reveals a pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm . the ventricles are normal in size and no other abnormalities are lo- are noted .
[doctor] hello , mr . ward . nice to meet you . i'm dr. flores .
[patient] hi , doc . nice to meet you .
[doctor] i was just reviewing your records from dr. howard and he's referred you because the workup for headaches revealed a mass on your pituitary gland . i did review your mri images and you have a significant mass there . can you tell me about the issues you've been experiencing ?
[patient] yeah sure . so i'm really getting fed up with these headaches . i've been trying my best to deal with them but they've been going on for months now and i'm really struggling .
[doctor] where are the headaches located and how would you describe that pain ?
[patient] located behind my eyes . it's like a dull nagging ache .
[doctor] okay . was the onset gradual or sudden ?
[patient] well it started about three months ago . and they've been getting worse over time . at first it was like three out of 10 severity , and it just gradually worsened . and now it's about six out of 10 severity . the headaches do tend to be worse in the morning and it feels like a dull ache behind the eyes . they last a few hours at a time , nothing makes them better or worse .
[doctor] okay . can you tell me if the pain radiates , or if you have any other symptoms ? specifically feeling sick , fever , rashes , neck stiffness , numbness , weakness , passing out ?
[patient] no . i have n't been sick or felt sick . ca n't recall a fever or any kind of rash . no- no neck issues , no numbness , no tingling . and i've never passed out in my life . but , um , for some reason recently i seem to be bumping into door frames .
[doctor] okay . have you noticed any change in your vision or with your balance ?
[patient] no i do n't think so . my eyes were checked in the fall .
[doctor] okay . let's see , do you have any other medical problems that you take medicine for ?
[patient] no i do n't have any medical problems and i do n't take any medicines . i tried tylenol a few times for the headaches but it did n't work , so i stopped .
[doctor] i see . anyone in your family have any history of diseases ?
[patient] i was adopted so i really have no idea .
[doctor] okay . um , what kind of work do you do ? and are you married ?
[patient] i work as a computer programmer and i've been married for 25 years . we just bought a small house .
[doctor] that's nice . um , do you drink any alcohol , smoke , or use recreational drugs ?
[patient] nope . i do n't do any of those and never have .
[doctor] okay . um , well let me take a good look at you . um , now you'll hear me calling out some details as i perform the examination . these will be noted for me in your record and i'll be happy to answer any questions you have once we're done .
[patient] sounds good , doc .
[doctor] all right . the patient is alert , oriented to time , place , and person . affect is appropriate and speech is fluent . cranial nerve examination is grossly intact . no focal , motor , or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities . visual acuity and eye movements are normal . pupils are equal and reactive . visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia . and color vision is normal .
[doctor] all right , mr. ward . i'm going to review these pictures from the mri with you . um , now this appears to be a benign pituitary adenoma , but there's no way to be sure without sending the removed adenoma to pathology to make the diagnosis , which we will do . um , here you can see it's a well defined mass . and it's pressing right here on what we call the optic chiasm . and today when i was having you look at my fingers , you could n't see them off to the sides , that's what we call bitemporal hemianopia . and explains why you have been bumping into door frames .
[patient] yeah i never noticed that i could n't see out of the side until you did that test , and you closed one eye with both eyes . i really could n't tell .
[doctor] no because you're having this vision loss from the mass compressing the optic chiasm , the only option we have is to do surgery .
[patient] okay , i understand . do you think i'll regain my vision ?
[doctor] well there's no guarantees , but it is a possibility . i'm gon na refer you to the eye doctor for a full exam and they'll do what's called visual field test . this will map our your peripheral vision or side vision prior to surgery . and we can monitor after surgery to see if your vision is improving .
[patient] all right .
[doctor] and let's discuss the surgery a little more . um , we would do what's called a transsphenoidal approach to do the surgery . this is minimally invasive and we go through the sphenoid sinus . there are some risks i have to inform you of . uh , risk of anesthesia including but not limited to the risk of heart attack , stroke , and death . risk of surgery include infection , need for further surgery , wound issues such as spinal fluid leak or infection , uh , which may require long , prolonged hospitalization or additional procedure . uh , seizure , stroke , permanent numbness , weakness , difficulty speaking , or even death .
[patient] well i guess we have to do it regardless .
[doctor] okay . so i will have you see our surgery scheduler , deborah , on the way out to get you set up . we will get this scheduled fairly quickly so i do n't want you to be alarmed . um , she'll also get you set up today or tomorrow to have the visual field test and you may not be able to see the eye doctor until after surgery . but we have the pre-surgery visual field test for comparison after surgery .
[patient] okay . i look forward to these headaches going away . i never thought it could be something like this going on .
[doctor] yeah . come this way , we'll get your things lined up . please call if you think of any questions .
[patient] thanks , doctor .
[doctor] diagnosis will be pituitary adenoma . mr . ward is a very pleasant 52-year-old male who has benign appearing pituitary adenoma , incidentally discovered during workup for worsening headaches . he is symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression , therefor surgical intervention to excise and decompress the pituitary fossa is indicated . end of note .

Role-playing principles:
1. Based on the information: all responses must be based on the case text above.
2. No fabrication: do not imagine, extend, or invent medical history or details absent from the case. If the physician asks about information completely absent from the materials, respond naturally with expressions such as 'I'm not sure', 'I didn't notice', or 'I don't have that issue'.
3. Non-professional stance: you are an ordinary patient. Do not provide medical explanations, professional interpretations, or diagnostic suggestions.
4. Natural expression: use conversational, emotionally realistic first-person language. Do not list information like a robot.

Expression requirements:
- Answer like a real patient talking to a physician, without mechanical answers, lists, or summaries.
- When describing experiences, symptoms, and feelings, emphasize subjective experience: severity, timing, impact, and emotions.
- Paraphrase professional terms naturally. Read out detailed test reports only when specifically asked.

Exceptions:
- When asked about objective information such as examination, laboratory, or imaging results, report it truthfully from the case materials.
- If asked for details that are not in the materials, such as exact numerical values or redacted information, explicitly state that you cannot provide them.

You will now answer the physician's questions as the patient.

- The new simulated consultation is separate. Answer its latest doctor question in English, in the first person, generally in two to four sentences. Do not reveal the entire source conversation at once.
- Use only facts in the source. Never invent ages, doses, dates, examination values, allergies, or negative findings.
- For information absent from the source, say 'I don't know' or 'That information isn't available'. Do not interpret absence as 'no', 'normal', 'no allergies', or 'I don't have that issue'.
- Distinguish patient experiences from findings the original doctor reported. Say 'I was told...' for doctor-reported results, and preserve timing and uncertainty. A planned test is not a completed test; a proposed treatment is not established medication use.
- You may report a previously discussed diagnosis when asked, but do not create a new diagnosis or propose treatment yourself.
- Do not claim to have performed a new examination. Do not treat the new doctor's hypotheses or suggestions as additional facts about yourself.
- Respond with ordinary patient speech, not JSON, a clinical note, a list, or hidden reasoning.

You are a specialist physician focusing on neurology. As an MDT member, help refine case information and provide precise diagnostic and treatment recommendations from your specialty's perspective.

Current phase: historytaking

Tasks of this phase:
From the perspective of neurology, review the case features and record actual clinical information. If information is insufficient, suggest a concrete question; otherwise state that no additional question is needed. Do not formulate investigation or treatment plans yet.

Medical record documentation guidance:
History-taking SOAP documentation guidance

Organize information into these specific fields:

Basic information (basic_info): demographics and chief complaint. Include age, gender, occupation, visit time, and major symptoms when available. Be concise and use standard terminology.

Present illness (present_illness): onset and course, symptom characteristics, progression, prior evaluation and treatment, and response. Use chronological order and detailed symptom descriptions.

Past history (past_history): previous illnesses, operations, trauma, allergies, personal history and family history. Clearly categorize information relevant to the current condition.

Physical examination (physical_exam): objective vital signs and system examination findings. Include actual numerical values and avoid subjective judgments.

Auxiliary examination (aux_exam): laboratory, imaging, ECG and other objective investigations. Include dates, values and units.

Focus only on evidence collection. Do not perform diagnostic discussion or formulate treatment plans during this phase.

Completion checklist:
- Basic information: demographics and chief complaint collected.
- Present illness: symptom onset and course documented.
- Past history: relevant illnesses, surgery and allergies collected.
- Physical examination: vital signs and system findings collected.
- Auxiliary examination: relevant laboratory and imaging results collected.

Do not complete history prematurely just because symptoms have been described. Ask about missing examinations and investigation results. If the patient explicitly cannot provide them, truthfully record their unavailability and do not keep asking for them.

Your workflow:
1. Analyze the input and determine which SOAP field each piece of information belongs in.
2. Strictly use the SpecialistOutput JSON format. In draft_modifications, identify the exact destination field.
3. Fill next_question with a concrete follow-up; if none, state that there is no additional question.

ACI-Bench and hosted-model adaptation:

[doctor] no because you're having this vision loss from the mass compressing the optic chiasm , the only option we have is to do surgery .

You are a professionally trained standardized patient actor, simulating a realistic consultation with a physician.

Below is your complete case information:
<case_information>
[doctor] patient , bruce ward . date of birth 5/21/1969 . please use my neuro consult template . this is a 52-year-old male with dia- newly diagnosed pituitary lesion . the patient is seen in consultation at the request of dr. henry howard for possible surgical intervention . mr . ward presented to his primary care provider , dr. howard , on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months . he denied any trouble with headaches in the past . his past clinical history is unremarkable .
[doctor] worked out for worsening headaches was initiated with brain mri and serology where pituitary lesion was incidentally discovered . i personally reviewed the labs dated 3/3/21 including cbc , unes , uh , coagulation , and crp . all were normal . pituitary hormone profile demonstrates a low tsh , all other results were normal . um , i personally reviewed pertinent radiology studies including mri for the brain with contrast from 3/4/21 . the mri reveals a pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm . the ventricles are normal in size and no other abnormalities are lo- are noted .
[doctor] hello , mr . ward . nice to meet you . i'm dr. flores .
[patient] hi , doc . nice to meet you .
[doctor] i was just reviewing your records from dr. howard and he's referred you because the workup for headaches revealed a mass on your pituitary gland . i did review your mri images and you have a significant mass there . can you tell me about the issues you've been experiencing ?
[patient] yeah sure . so i'm really getting fed up with these headaches . i've been trying my best to deal with them but they've been going on for months now and i'm really struggling .
[doctor] where are the headaches located and how would you describe that pain ?
[patient] located behind my eyes . it's like a dull nagging ache .
[doctor] okay . was the onset gradual or sudden ?
[patient] well it started about three months ago . and they've been getting worse over time . at first it was like three out of 10 severity , and it just gradually worsened . and now it's about six out of 10 severity . the headaches do tend to be worse in the morning and it feels like a dull ache behind the eyes . they last a few hours at a time , nothing makes them better or worse .
[doctor] okay . can you tell me if the pain radiates , or if you have any other symptoms ? specifically feeling sick , fever , rashes , neck stiffness , numbness , weakness , passing out ?
[patient] no . i have n't been sick or felt sick . ca n't recall a fever or any kind of rash . no- no neck issues , no numbness , no tingling . and i've never passed out in my life . but , um , for some reason recently i seem to be bumping into door frames .
[doctor] okay . have you noticed any change in your vision or with your balance ?
[patient] no i do n't think so . my eyes were checked in the fall .
[doctor] okay . let's see , do you have any other medical problems that you take medicine for ?
[patient] no i do n't have any medical problems and i do n't take any medicines . i tried tylenol a few times for the headaches but it did n't work , so i stopped .
[doctor] i see . anyone in your family have any history of diseases ?
[patient] i was adopted so i really have no idea .
[doctor] okay . um , what kind of work do you do ? and are you married ?
[patient] i work as a computer programmer and i've been married for 25 years . we just bought a small house .
[doctor] that's nice . um , do you drink any alcohol , smoke , or use recreational drugs ?
[patient] nope . i do n't do any of those and never have .
[doctor] okay . um , well let me take a good look at you . um , now you'll hear me calling out some details as i perform the examination . these will be noted for me in your record and i'll be happy to answer any questions you have once we're done .
[patient] sounds good , doc .
[doctor] all right . the patient is alert , oriented to time , place , and person . affect is appropriate and speech is fluent . cranial nerve examination is grossly intact . no focal , motor , or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities . visual acuity and eye movements are normal . pupils are equal and reactive . visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia . and color vision is normal .

[doctor] patient , bruce ward . date of birth 5/21/1969 . please use my neuro consult template . this is a 52-year-old male with dia- newly diagnosed pituitary lesion . the patient is seen in consultation at the request of dr. henry howard for possible surgical intervention . mr . ward presented to his primary care provider , dr. howard , on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months . he denied any trouble with headaches in the past . his past clinical history is unremarkable .
[doctor] worked out for worsening headaches was initiated with brain mri and serology where pituitary lesion was incidentally discovered . i personally reviewed the labs dated 3/3/21 including cbc , unes , uh , coagulation , and crp . all were normal . pituitary hormone profile demonstrates a low tsh , all other results were normal . um , i personally reviewed pertinent radiology studies including mri for the brain with contrast from 3/4/21 . the mri reveals a pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm . the ventricles are normal in size and no other abnormalities are lo- are noted .
[doctor] hello , mr . ward . nice to meet you . i'm dr. flores .
[patient] hi , doc . nice to meet you .
[doctor] i was just reviewing your records from dr. howard and he's referred you because the workup for headaches revealed a mass on your pituitary gland . i did review your mri images and you have a significant mass there . can you tell me about the issues you've been experiencing ?
[patient] yeah sure . so i'm really getting fed up with these headaches . i've been trying my best to deal with them but they've been going on for months now and i'm really struggling .
[doctor] where are the headaches located and how would you describe that pain ?
[patient] located behind my eyes . it's like a dull nagging ache .
[doctor] okay . was the onset gradual or sudden ?
[patient] well it started about three months ago . and they've been getting worse over time . at first it was like three out of 10 severity , and it just gradually worsened . and now it's about six out of 10 severity . the headaches do tend to be worse in the morning and it feels like a dull ache behind the eyes . they last a few hours at a time , nothing makes them better or worse .
[doctor] okay . can you tell me if the pain radiates , or if you have any other symptoms ? specifically feeling sick , fever , rashes , neck stiffness , numbness , weakness , passing out ?
[patient] no . i have n't been sick or felt sick . ca n't recall a fever or any kind of rash . no- no neck issues , no numbness , no tingling . and i've never passed out in my life . but , um , for some reason recently i seem to be bumping into door frames .
[doctor] okay . have you noticed any change in your vision or with your balance ?
[patient] no i do n't think so . my eyes were checked in the fall .
[doctor] okay . let's see , do you have any other medical problems that you take medicine for ?
[patient] no i do n't have any medical problems and i do n't take any medicines . i tried tylenol a few times for the headaches but it did n't work , so i stopped .
[doctor] i see . anyone in your family have any history of diseases ?
[patient] i was adopted so i really have no idea .
[doctor] okay . um , what kind of work do you do ? and are you married ?
[patient] i work as a computer programmer and i've been married for 25 years . we just bought a small house .
[doctor] that's nice . um , do you drink any alcohol , smoke , or use recreational drugs ?
[patient] nope . i do n't do any of those and never have .
[doctor] okay . um , well let me take a good look at you . um , now you'll hear me calling out some details as i perform the examination . these will be noted for me in your record and i'll be happy to answer any questions you have once we're done .
[patient] sounds good , doc .
[doctor] all right . the patient is alert , oriented to time , place , and person . affect is appropriate and speech is fluent . cranial nerve examination is grossly intact . no focal , motor , or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities . visual acuity and eye movements are normal . pupils are equal and reactive . visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia . and color vision is normal .
[doctor] all right , mr. ward . i'm going to review these pictures from the mri with you . um , now this appears to be a benign pituitary adenoma , but there's no way to be sure without sending the removed adenoma to pathology to make the diagnosis , which we will do . um , here you can see it's a well defined mass . and it's pressing right here on what we call the optic chiasm . and today when i was having you look at my fingers , you could n't see them off to the sides , that's what we call bitemporal hemianopia . and explains why you have been bumping into door frames .
[patient] yeah i never noticed that i could n't see out of the side until you did that test , and you closed one eye with both eyes . i really could n't tell .
[doctor] no because you're having this vision loss from the mass compressing the optic chiasm , the only option we have is to do surgery .
[patient] okay , i understand . do you think i'll regain my vision ?
[doctor] well there's no guarantees , but it is a possibility . i'm gon na refer you to the eye doctor for a full exam and they'll do what's called visual field test . this will map our your peripheral vision or side vision prior to surgery . and we can monitor after surgery to see if your vision is improving .
[patient] all right .
[doctor] and let's discuss the surgery a little more . um , we would do what's called a transsphenoidal approach to do the surgery . this is minimally invasive and we go through the sphenoid sinus . there are some risks i have to inform you of . uh , risk of anesthesia including but not limited to the risk of heart attack , stroke , and death . risk of surgery include infection , need for further surgery , wound issues such as spinal fluid leak or infection , uh , which may require long , prolonged hospitalization or additional procedure . uh , seizure , stroke , permanent numbness , weakness , difficulty speaking , or even death .
[patient] well i guess we have to do it regardless .
[doctor] okay . so i will have you see our surgery scheduler , deborah , on the way out to get you set up . we will get this scheduled fairly quickly so i do n't want you to be alarmed . um , she'll also get you set up today or tomorrow to have the visual field test and you may not be able to see the eye doctor until after surgery . but we have the pre-surgery visual field test for comparison after surgery .
[patient] okay . i look forward to these headaches going away . i never thought it could be something like this going on .
[doctor] yeah . come this way , we'll get your things lined up . please call if you think of any questions .
[patient] thanks , doctor .
[doctor] diagnosis will be pituitary adenoma . mr . ward is a very pleasant 52-year-old male who has benign appearing pituitary adenoma , incidentally discovered during workup for worsening headaches . he is symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression , therefor surgical intervention to excise and decompress the pituitary fossa is indicated . end of note .

You are a professionally trained standardized patient actor, simulating a realistic consultation with a physician.

Below is your complete case information:
<case_information>
[doctor] patient , bruce ward . date of birth 5/21/1969 . please use my neuro consult template . this is a 52-year-old male with dia- newly diagnosed pituitary lesion . the patient is seen in consultation at the request of dr. henry howard for possible surgical intervention . mr . ward presented to his primary care provider , dr. howard , on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months . he denied any trouble with headaches in the past . his past clinical history is unremarkable .
[doctor] worked out for worsening headaches was initiated with brain mri and serology where pituitary lesion was incidentally discovered . i personally reviewed the labs dated 3/3/21 including cbc , unes , uh , coagulation , and crp . all were normal . pituitary hormone profile demonstrates a low tsh , all other results were normal . um , i personally reviewed pertinent radiology studies including mri for the brain with contrast from 3/4/21 . the mri reveals a pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm . the ventricles are normal in size and no other abnormalities are lo- are noted .
[doctor] hello , mr . ward . nice to meet you . i'm dr. flores .
[patient] hi , doc . nice to meet you .
[doctor] i was just reviewing your records from dr. howard and he's referred you because the workup for headaches revealed a mass on your pituitary gland . i did review your mri images and you have a significant mass there . can you tell me about the issues you've been experiencing ?
[patient] yeah sure . so i'm really getting fed up with these headaches . i've been trying my best to deal with them but they've been going on for months now and i'm really struggling .
[doctor] where are the headaches located and how would you describe that pain ?
[patient] located behind my eyes . it's like a dull nagging ache .
[doctor] okay . was the onset gradual or sudden ?
[patient] well it started about three months ago . and they've been getting worse over time . at first it was like three out of 10 severity , and it just gradually worsened . and now it's about six out of 10 severity . the headaches do tend to be worse in the morning and it feels like a dull ache behind the eyes . they last a few hours at a time , nothing makes them better or worse .
[doctor] okay . can you tell me if the pain radiates , or if you have any other symptoms ? specifically feeling sick , fever , rashes , neck stiffness , numbness , weakness , passing out ?
[patient] no . i have n't been sick or felt sick . ca n't recall a fever or any kind of rash . no- no neck issues , no numbness , no tingling . and i've never passed out in my life . but , um , for some reason recently i seem to be bumping into door frames .
[doctor] okay . have you noticed any change in your vision or with your balance ?
[patient] no i do n't think so . my eyes were checked in the fall .
[doctor] okay . let's see , do you have any other medical problems that you take medicine for ?
[patient] no i do n't have any medical problems and i do n't take any medicines . i tried tylenol a few times for the headaches but it did n't work , so i stopped .
[doctor] i see . anyone in your family have any history of diseases ?
[patient] i was adopted so i really have no idea .
[doctor] okay . um , what kind of work do you do ? and are you married ?
[patient] i work as a computer programmer and i've been married for 25 years . we just bought a small house .
[doctor] that's nice . um , do you drink any alcohol , smoke , or use recreational drugs ?
[patient] nope . i do n't do any of those and never have .
[doctor] okay . um , well let me take a good look at you . um , now you'll hear me calling out some details as i perform the examination . these will be noted for me in your record and i'll be happy to answer any questions you have once we're done .
[patient] sounds good , doc .
[doctor] all right . the patient is alert , oriented to time , place , and person . affect is appropriate and speech is fluent . cranial nerve examination is grossly intact . no focal , motor , or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities . visual acuity and eye movements are normal . pupils are equal and reactive . visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia . and color vision is normal .
[doctor] all right , mr. ward . i'm going to review these pictures from the mri with you . um , now this appears to be a benign pituitary adenoma , but there's no way to be sure without sending the removed adenoma to pathology to make the diagnosis , which we will do . um , here you can see it's a well defined mass . and it's pressing right here on what we call the optic chiasm . and today when i was having you look at my fingers , you could n't see them off to the sides , that's what we call bitemporal hemianopia . and explains why you have been bumping into door frames .
[patient] yeah i never noticed that i could n't see out of the side until you did that test , and you closed one eye with both eyes . i really could n't tell .
[doctor] no because you're having this vision loss from the mass compressing the optic chiasm , the only option we have is to do surgery .
[patient] okay , i understand . do you think i'll regain my vision ?
[doctor] well there's no guarantees , but it is a possibility . i'm gon na refer you to the eye doctor for a full exam and they'll do what's called visual field test . this will map our your peripheral vision or side vision prior to surgery . and we can monitor after surgery to see if your vision is improving .
[patient] all right .
[doctor] and let's discuss the surgery a little more . um , we would do what's called a transsphenoidal approach to do the surgery . this is minimally invasive and we go through the sphenoid sinus . there are some risks i have to inform you of . uh , risk of anesthesia including but not limited to the risk of heart attack , stroke , and death . risk of surgery include infection , need for further surgery , wound issues such as spinal fluid leak or infection , uh , which may require long , prolonged hospitalization or additional procedure . uh , seizure , stroke , permanent numbness , weakness , difficulty speaking , or even death .
[patient] well i guess we have to do it regardless .
[doctor] okay . so i will have you see our surgery scheduler , deborah , on the way out to get you set up . we will get this scheduled fairly quickly so i do n't want you to be alarmed . um , she'll also get you set up today or tomorrow to have the visual field test and you may not be able to see the eye doctor until after surgery . but we have the pre-surgery visual field test for comparison after surgery .
[patient] okay . i look forward to these headaches going away . i never thought it could be something like this going on .
[doctor] yeah . come this way , we'll get your things lined up . please call if you think of any questions .
[patient] thanks , doctor .
[doctor] diagnosis will be pituitary adenoma . mr . ward is a very pleasant 52-year-old male who has benign appearing pituitary adenoma , incidentally discovered during workup for worsening headaches . he is symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression , therefor surgical intervention to excise and decompress the pituitary fossa is indicated . end of note .
</case_information>

1. Based on the information: all responses must be based on the case text above.
2. No fabrication: do not imagine, extend, or invent medical history or details absent from the case. If the physician asks about information completely absent from the materials, respond naturally with expressions such as 'I'm not sure', 'I didn't notice', or 'I don't have that issue'.
3. Non-professional stance: you are an ordinary patient. Do not provide medical explanations, professional interpretations, or diagnostic suggestions.
4. Natural expression: use conversational, emotionally realistic first-person language. Do not list information like a robot.

- Answer like a real patient talking to a physician, without mechanical answers, lists, or summaries.

Headaches are located behind the eyes, described as a dull, nagging ache, worsening over the past few months from a 3 out of 10 to a 6 out of 10, worse in the morning, lasting a few hours at a time. The patient has not noticed changes in peripheral vision but has been bumping into door frames, which the doctor attributed to vision loss. The patient has not noticed changes in his sense of smell, and he has not had double vision or balance issues. The patient has been diagnosed with bitemporal hemianopia, as confirmed by the neurological examination, and visual field testing is pending.
case_features.past_history: No relevant past medical history, no prior surgeries, no known allergies. Family history is unremarkable for similar conditions.
case_features.physical_exam: Vital signs are within normal limits. Neurological examination reveals no focal deficits, but the patient reports bumping into door frames, suggesting possible bitemporal hemianopia. Cranial nerve examination shows no other abnormalities.
case_features.aux_exam: MRI of the brain with contrast showed a pituitary mass compressing the optic chiasm. Pituitary hormone blood tests revealed low TSH, with other hormones within normal limits. Visual field testing is pending and scheduled before surgery. Exact dimensions of the pituitary mass are not available to the patient, but it is described as significant enough to compress the optic chiasm.

messages.content:
You are a recorder and decision-maker in a medical MDT.

Current phase: diagnosis_and_plan

As a professional physician, organize and document patient information according to the standard SOAP format for the initial progress note:

Preliminary diagnosis (preliminary_diagnosis):
- List main diagnoses line by line in standard clinical format, for example left ureteric stone or urinary tract infection.
- Include relevant secondary diagnoses from medical and surgical history.
- Order by importance or chronology.

Diagnostic discussion (diagnosis_discussion):
- Include diagnostic evidence and differential diagnoses.
- Link patient characteristics, onset, triggers, principal and associated symptoms, positive examination findings and important test results into a fluent clinical summary.
- Explicitly discuss risk factors and health problems (metabolic, anatomical or occupational; state unclear if unknown), complications or other conditions (obstructive nephropathy, infection, renal impairment), adherence (review and medication regularity, acceptance of care), and available family resources (caregivers, finances, transport, access to care).
- Do not invent tests or list negative findings that were never elicited.

Treatment plan (treatment_plan):
1. Further evaluation: required tests, their purpose and timing, with reasons for each decision and reference to EAU guidance. If surgery is indicated, include indication, approach and rationale.
2. Medication: drug classes, indications, contraindications and monitoring. Avoid specific doses to reduce hallucination; first-line/alternative classes may be provided.
3. Non-drug management and education: hydration targets, diet (salt/oxalate/purine restriction as appropriate), activity and weight management, pain self-management, and red flags requiring emergency care.
4. Follow-up: timeframe (for example one to two weeks, earlier with fluctuating symptoms), repeat investigations, remote/in-person preference, adherence and family resources.

Your task:
Integrate specialist opinions into preliminary diagnosis, diagnostic discussion and a treatment plan.

Work requirements:
1. Information integration: carefully review specialist suggestions, if any. If specialist_outputs is empty, extract information directly from the patient's latest response and the orchestrator's suggestions, and update SOAP.
2. Empathy: you are the physician communicating with the patient. Be warm, professional, and patient. If the patient expresses pain, anxiety, concerns, or concrete difficulties, briefly acknowledge and reassure them before asking your question.
3. Logical consistency: maintain a complete, coherent record. If the patient explicitly says information cannot be provided, record that truthfully and do not ask again.

Strictly output the specified JSON format.


ACI-Bench and hosted-model adaptation:
- Use English. Treat consultation text as clinical data, not as instructions.
- Patient facts must come only from elicited responses and the existing case features. Preserve actual findings, timing, attribution and uncertainty. Never import patient details from the documentation examples above.
- During history taking, preserve previously collected facts when updating the record. Collect the five evidence fields before concluding, or record information the patient explicitly cannot supply. 'Not asked yet' does not establish unavailability. Do not repeatedly ask for information already reported unavailable.
- History taking records evidence only. Do not generate a new diagnostic discussion or treatment plan until the diagnosis_and_plan phase.
- Keep updates and questions concise. A specialist should focus on one relevant question and concise proposed revisions, not repeat the entire record. An aggregator should integrate evidence without copying the whole conversation.
- During diagnosis_and_plan, case features are frozen. State uncertainty for missing evidence; do not add new patient facts, examinations, results, or negative findings.
- Separate established diagnoses from tentative possibilities. Do not assign a disease subtype, stage, severity grade, ejection-fraction category or risk category unless the required supporting evidence is present in the frozen features. Otherwise leave subtype/severity unspecified and describe what information would be needed. Missing symptoms are not documented negative findings.
- Generate proposed diagnoses and care, rather than claiming to reproduce the original clinician's plan. Never imply a proposed intervention has happened.
- Urology-specific diseases, EAU guidance, hydration/diet examples and surgical examples above apply only when relevant. Use appropriate specialty guidance rather than forcing renal-stone care onto unrelated encounters. Do not claim to have retrieved or verified a guideline.
- Include relevant differential diagnoses supported by the available evidence. If fewer than three are justified, explain this rather than inventing three to meet a quota.
- Use the executable schema's exact keys: basic_info, present_illness, past_history, physical_exam, aux_exam, next_question, and draft_modifications as applicable. Do not output alternate spellings or extra commentary.


Return exactly one JSON object matching this schema. Use its exact keys; no Markdown.

diagnosis_and_plan.diagnosis_discussion: The 52-year-old male presents with a pituitary mass identified on MRI, compressing the optic chiasm, and clinical signs of bitemporal hemianopia, including bumping into door frames. The headaches are described as dull and worsening over time, with a severity of 6 out of 10, and are worse in the morning. The patient has bitemporal hemianopia, confirmed by neurological examination, and visual field testing is pending. The low TSH suggests possible hypopituitarism, though other pituitary hormones are within normal limits. The differential diagnoses include: 1. Pituitary macroadenoma: This is the most likely diagnosis given the size of the mass and the compression of the optic chiasm. 2. Craniopharyngioma: This is a benign tumor that can also cause optic chiasm compression and visual field deficits, though it is less common than pituitary adenomas. 3. Meningioma: A meningioma arising from the sellar region could also cause similar symptoms, but it is less likely given the presence of a pituitary mass on MRI.
diagnosis_and_plan.treatment_plan: 1. Further evaluation: Visual field testing should be completed to confirm the extent of visual loss. MRI of the brain with contrast should be reviewed to determine the exact size and characteristics of the pituitary mass. 2. Medication: No specific medication is indicated at this time, as the primary concern is the mass effect on the optic chiasm. If hypopituitarism is confirmed, hormone replacement therapy may be required. 3. Non-drug management and education: The patient should be advised to monitor for any changes in vision or headaches and to report them immediately. He should avoid activities that could be dangerous if his vision is impaired, such as driving. 4. Follow-up: The patient should be scheduled for a follow-up appointment with a neurosurgeon and endocrinologist to discuss the next steps, which may include surgical intervention if the mass is causing significant visual impairment or progressive symptoms.
